t: Find All Lonely Numbers in the Array — Frequencies Plus Neighbor Checks
o: A value x is lonely when its frequency is exactly 1 AND neither neighbor x − 1 nor x + 1 appears anywhere in the array. In example 1 ([10,6,5,8]) values 5 and 6 are adjacent integers, so neither qualifies; 10 and 8 stand alone. In example 2 ([1,3,5,3]) the value 3 fails purely on frequency since it appears twice, even though no neighbor exists, leaving [1,5]. With n up to 10⁵, testing each x by rescanning the array is O(n²); a hash map answers all presence queries in O(1), and a sorted pass answers them via adjacent gaps instead.
k: Two independent conditions must hold: frequency(x) == 1 AND both neighbors x ± 1 absent.
A frequency map turns each loneliness test into three O(1) average-time lookups.
Sorting clusters adjacent values together, so gaps strictly larger than 1 on both sides certify loneliness — duplicates produce gap 0 and self-reject.

a.i: Count every value once, then walk the distinct keys emitting each x whose count is 1 and whose immediate integer neighbors are missing from the map. Output order is free per the problem statement.
s: Build cnt[x] = frequency over nums in one pass.
For each distinct x, require cnt[x] == 1.
Verify x − 1 and x + 1 are absent from cnt.
Append surviving x values to the result list.
a.t: O(n) — one counting pass plus one pass over distinct values with O(1) average lookups.

a.i: In a sorted copy, x is lonely precisely when its left neighbor differs by more than 1 and its right neighbor differs by more than 1. Equal duplicates sit at gap 0 and disqualify themselves automatically, so no separate frequency check is needed.
s: Sort a copy s of nums.
For each index i check s[i] − s[i−1] > 1 (or i == 0) and s[i+1] − s[i] > 1 (or i is last).
Collect the passing values as the answer.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates the linear scan.
a.sp: O(n) for the sorted copy (O(1) extra if sorting in place is acceptable).

w: The hash-map solution is the interview default; bring up the sort variant when memory is tight or ordered output is desired. Traps: forgetting the frequency == 1 clause (duplicates like the two 3s in example 2 must be rejected even though their neighbors are absent), and checking adjacency on only one side. Since values cap at 10⁶, a direct boolean-array encoding (freq[], present[]) is also viable and beats hashing constants-wise. Follow-ups: report lonely numbers within a query range, or handle streams where counts arrive incrementally.
